sections.h2: What does a Tennessee quitclaim deed do?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed passes whatever interest the signer holds in the parcel and makes no promise that the interest is good. The Tennessee Department of Revenue draws that line when it explains recording tax: a true quitclaim conveys a "mere chance of title," while a deed that conveys the property itself or gives a warranty is treated differently.

Owners in Tennessee use the form for transfers inside a family, for adding or removing a spouse, and for clearing a name from a chain of ownership. Because no warranty comes with it, a buyer who takes a quitclaim deed from a stranger relies entirely on the title search. That matters if you plan to sell: a house whose last transfer was a quitclaim will draw closer questions from a title company than one with a warranty deed behind it.

The deed still has to be recorded with the county register of deeds, and recording is where Tennessee's tax, fee and formatting rules apply. The sections below follow that path from the tax base to the counter at the register's office.

sections.h2: How much recording tax does a Tennessee quitclaim deed carry?
sections.html:
The realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100, or $3.70 per $1,000, and the grantee pays it through the register of deeds in the county where the deed is offered for recording. The Department of Revenue rate page lists the same figure, and the register forwards the money to the state.

What changes for a quitclaim is the base the rate is applied to. The Shelby County Register's guide says the tax on a quitclaim uses only the consideration actually given, and it cites Tenn. Code Ann. 67-4-409(a)(1)(D). A quitclaim given for $10 to a relative would therefore carry a very small bill. A deed with wording that reaches for the property itself would be taxed on its value instead.

How the wording of a deed sets the tax base
Deed situationTax baseSource
True quitclaim that passes only the signer's chance of titleConsideration givenRevenue help article REC-20; Shelby County Register
Quitclaim that uses a habendum clause ("to have and to hold") or "in fee simple (absolute)"Fair market value of the propertyRevenue help article REC-20
Quitclaim in a transaction the statute exemptsNo tax, and no oath of valueShelby County Register, citing 67-4-409(a)(1)(E)

For a house worth $250,000 that is conveyed on a deed taxed at full value, the tax would be $925 (250,000 times 0.0037). The same house moved on a true quitclaim for $10 of consideration would carry a few cents of tax at the same rate, and the register's fees would still apply.

sections.h2: Which quitclaim wording pushes the tax to fair market value?
sections.html:
Language that signals an intent to convey the land itself, or that gives a warranty, moves the tax base from consideration to fair market value. Revenue's examples are a habendum clause and the phrase "in fee simple (absolute)," and it says the list is not limited to those two.

That is a drafting issue for whoever prepares the deed. If you are given a form from the internet and it contains warranty-style phrases, ask the preparer to remove them or expect the register to charge on value. A deed prepared by an attorney or a title company should already be consistent with the tax treatment you expect.

  • Check the granting clause for words that promise title.
  • Look for a habendum clause or fee simple language.
  • Confirm the consideration stated matches what was actually given.
  • Ask the register of deeds to explain the tax before you leave the deed behind.

sections.h2: How does Tennessee decide fair market value when the deed is taxed on value?
sections.html:
Revenue accepts the tax base listed in the local assessor's office, or a recent appraisal that the assessor's office has accepted when the base is being disputed. Anything lower is open to audit by the Department, with penalties and interest added to any tax found due.

In practice that means the appraised value on your county's assessment roll is the safe starting number. If you believe the assessor's figure is too high, the appraisal route exists, but it has to be one the assessor has accepted. Ask the county property assessor for the current appraisal of your parcel before the deed is drawn, so the oath on the deed and the tax paid line up.

sections.h2: What does the register of deeds require before recording a quitclaim deed?
sections.html:
The Shelby County Register publishes a checklist that cites the statutes behind each item, and it is a good model for any Tennessee county. A quitclaim deed is listed among the taxable title transfer documents, and the register's list marks every item below as applying to it.

  • Names of the grantor and the grantee (Tenn. Code Ann. 8-13-108(a)(3)).
  • An affidavit of value when the deed is taxable (67-4-409(a)(6)(A)).
  • A derivation clause (66-24-110) and the property address unless the land is vacant (66-24-113(b)).
  • The name and address of the property owner, and of whoever pays the real property taxes (66-24-114).
  • The ward, block and parcel number (66-24-122) and a legal description.
  • The name and address of the person who prepared the deed (66-24-115).
  • Proper acknowledgments (66-22-101) and an original document, unless filed electronically.

The Davidson County Register of Deeds adds a plain rule on its fee page: every document except releases and charters must show the name and address of its preparer. Call the register's office in the county where the house sits to confirm how it takes submissions before you travel with a deed.

sections.h2: What does recording a quitclaim deed cost in Davidson and Shelby counties?
sections.html:
Recording fees come from Tenn. Code Ann. 8-21-1001, and the two largest counties publish them in similar terms. Davidson County lists warranty and quitclaim deeds under "all other documents" at $5 per page with a $10 minimum, plus a $2 data processing fee. Shelby County charges $10 for the first two pages and $5 for each additional page, with a data processing fee on top.

  • Davidson County: $1 probate fee, collected only when state tax is paid.
  • Shelby County: $1 register fee, collected only when state tax is collected.
  • Both counties: the $0.37 per $100 transfer tax is separate from these fees.

Other counties publish their own schedules. Ask the register of deeds in the county where the house sits for the current schedule.

sections.h2: Which Tennessee transfers escape the recording tax?
sections.html:
Tennessee exempts several transfers, and the Shelby County guide lists them with citations to 67-4-409(a)(1). Where a transaction is exempt, no oath of value is required.

  • A conveyance from one spouse to the other that creates or dissolves a tenancy by the entirety.
  • Domestic settlement decrees and deeds that adjust property rights between divorcing parties.
  • Transfers into a revocable living trust by the person who created it or by a spouse, and transfers back out to the same people.
  • Deeds an executor signs to carry out a testamentary devise.
  • Release of a life estate to the holders of the remainder interest.

An exemption does not remove the register's fee schedule or the formatting rules above. It only removes the transfer tax and the oath of value.

sections.h2: Did Tennessee change what the register can accept in 2026?
sections.html:
Yes. Public Chapter 865 of 2026 amends Tenn. Code Ann. 66-24-101(a), and it took effect on April 27, 2026. The University of Tennessee's County Technical Assistance Service summarizes it in its 2026 index of acts.

Under the act, a bond for the conveyance of real or personal property must carry authenticated signatures of all parties and the bond's expiration date to be eligible for recording. Agreements for the conveyance of real property, contracts, memoranda and abstracts for the sale of real property must carry authenticated signatures of the owner (or the owner's attorney-in-fact or court-appointed representative) and the proposed purchaser, along with an expiration date. A quitclaim deed is a different instrument, but sellers who record a purchase contract or memorandum should know the standard has tightened.

faqs.q: Who pays the Tennessee transfer tax on a quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: The grantee pays it. Revenue's help article says the tax is paid by the grantee shown on the instrument and collected by the register of the county where the deed is offered for recording.

faqs.q: Do I have to swear to the value on a quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Yes, when the deed is taxable. The Shelby County Register lists an affidavit of value for taxable deeds, citing 67-4-409(a)(6)(A), and says no oath is required in a transaction the statute exempts.

faqs.q: Can spouses use a quitclaim deed without paying the tax?
faqs.a: A conveyance from one spouse to the other that creates or dissolves a tenancy by the entirety is on the exemption list, as are divorce-related deeds. The list is narrow, so confirm your facts with the register or an attorney.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Nashville?
faqs.a: Davidson County charges $5 per page with a $10 minimum and a $2 data processing fee, plus the transfer tax and a $1 probate fee when state tax is paid. Page count and tax drive the total.

faqs.q: Will the register accept a photocopy of my quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Usually no. Shelby County requires an original document unless the filing is made electronically. Ask your county register about its e-filing option before you send anything.
